questiontext.text: A ball is travelling with uniform translatory motion. This means that

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Translatory motion is characterized by every particle of a rigid body shifting along parallel trajectories such that any line segment connecting two points in the body remains parallel to its initial orientation at all times.

Step 2: Condition for Uniformity
For translatory motion to be uniform, the velocity of the body must remain constant in both magnitude and direction over time. This requires the net acceleration of the object to be zero.

Step 3: Rotational Exclusion
If the body were spinning about an axis or rotating about its centre of mass, different points on the body would possess different tangential velocities. Pure translatory motion precludes any rotation or spin, thereby ensuring that all constituent particles of the object possess identical linear velocity vectors at every instant.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
A state of rest is merely a special static case with zero speed, whereas uniform translatory motion permits non-zero constant velocity. A circular path requires centripetal acceleration, which constantly changes velocity direction. Thus, uniform translatory motion requires all parts of the ball to share an identical, constant velocity vector.
Final conceptual result: all parts of the ball have the same velocity (magnitude and direction) and the velocity is constant.

answer.text: it is at rest.
the path can be a straight line or circular and the ball travels with uniform speed.
all parts of the ball have the same velocity (magnitude and direction) and the velocity is constant.
the centre of the ball moves with constant velocity and the ball spins about its centre uniformly.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQI_LAWS_OF_MOTION_MCQ_Q02 - Conditions for uniform velocity of metre scale

questiontext.text: A metre scale is moving with uniform velocity. This implies

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Uniform velocity means that the linear velocity vector \(\mathbf{v}\) of the centre of mass of the metre scale is constant in both magnitude and direction, and the scale does not rotate.

Step 2: Linear Equilibrium
According to Newton's second law for a rigid body, the net external force is proportional to the linear acceleration of its centre of mass: \[\mathbf{F}_{\text{net}} = m\frac{d\mathbf{v}}{dt}\] Because the velocity is uniform, \(\frac{d\mathbf{v}}{dt} = \mathbf{0}\), which implies the resultant external force acting on the scale must be zero.

Step 3: Rotational Equilibrium
If a non-zero net torque were acting about the centre of mass, the metre scale would experience angular acceleration according to \(\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\text{net}} = I\boldsymbol{\alpha}\). This would introduce rotation, causing the linear velocities of different points along the scale to vary and change continuously with time. Thus, to maintain uniform velocity without rotation, the net torque acting about the centre of mass must also be zero.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Both translational equilibrium and rotational equilibrium must simultaneously hold for an extended body moving with steady linear velocity.
Final conceptual result: the force acting on the scale is zero and the torque acting about centre of mass of the scale is also zero.

answer.text: the force acting on the scale is zero, but a torque about the centre of mass can act on the scale.
the force acting on the scale is zero and the torque acting about centre of mass of the scale is also zero.
the total force acting on it need not be zero but the torque on it is zero.
neither the force nor the torque need to be zero.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQI_LAWS_OF_MOTION_MCQ_Q03 - Change in momentum of cricket ball

questiontext.text: A cricket ball of mass \(150\,\text{g}\) has an initial velocity \(\mathbf{u} = (3\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 4\hat{\mathbf{j}})\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) and a final velocity \(\mathbf{v} = -(3\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 4\hat{\mathbf{j}})\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) after being hit. The change in momentum (final momentum \(-\) initial momentum) is (in \(\text{kg m s}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of cricket ball: \(m = 150\,\text{g} = 0.15\,\text{kg}\).
Initial velocity: \(\mathbf{u} = (3\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 4\hat{\mathbf{j}})\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
Final velocity: \(\mathbf{v} = -(3\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 4\hat{\mathbf{j}})\,\text{m s}^{-1} = (-3\hat{\mathbf{i}} - 4\hat{\mathbf{j}})\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Change in linear momentum is defined by: \[\Delta \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{p}_f - \mathbf{p}_i = m(\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{u})\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Subtract the initial velocity vector from the final velocity vector: \[\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{u} = (-3\hat{\mathbf{i}} - 4\hat{\mathbf{j}}) - (3\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 4\hat{\mathbf{j}}) = -6\hat{\mathbf{i}} - 8\hat{\mathbf{j}}\,\text{m s}^{-1}\] Multiply by the mass in kilograms: \[\Delta \mathbf{p} = 0.15 \times (-6\hat{\mathbf{i}} - 8\hat{\mathbf{j}}) = -(0.9\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 1.2\hat{\mathbf{j}})\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Both rectangular components reverse completely, doubling in the negative direction, yielding \(-0.9\hat{\mathbf{i}} - 1.2\hat{\mathbf{j}}\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\).
Final conceptual result: \(-(0.9\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 1.2\hat{\mathbf{j}})\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQI_LAWS_OF_MOTION_MCQ_Q04 - Magnitude of momentum transferred to cricket ball

questiontext.text: In the previous problem (5.3), the magnitude of the momentum transferred during the hit is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
From the previous calculation, the vector change in momentum of the cricket ball is: \[\Delta \mathbf{p} = -(0.9\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 1.2\hat{\mathbf{j}})\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\]

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The magnitude of a two-dimensional vector \(\mathbf{A} = A_x\hat{\mathbf{i}} + A_y\hat{\mathbf{j}}\) is evaluated as: \[|\mathbf{A}| = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the components of \(\Delta \mathbf{p}\): \[|\Delta \mathbf{p}| = \sqrt{(-0.9)^2 + (-1.2)^2}\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\] \[|\Delta \mathbf{p}| = \sqrt{0.81 + 1.44} = \sqrt{2.25} = 1.5\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The magnitude is strictly non-negative and equals \(1.5\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\), which correctly reflects the momentum transferred to the ball during the impact.
Final conceptual result: \(1.5\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQI_LAWS_OF_MOTION_MCQ_Q05 - Derivation of momentum conservation from Newtons laws

questiontext.text: Conservation of momentum in a collision between particles can be understood from

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Consider two particles colliding during a short time interval \(\Delta t\). Let \(\mathbf{F}_{12}\) be the force exerted on particle 1 by particle 2, and \(\mathbf{F}_{21}\) be the force exerted on particle 2 by particle 1.

Step 2: Role of Newton's Second Law
Newton's second law relates the force on each particle to its rate of change of momentum: \[\Delta \mathbf{p}_1 = \mathbf{F}_{12}\Delta t \quad \text{and} \quad \Delta \mathbf{p}_2 = \mathbf{F}_{21}\Delta t\]

Step 3: Role of Newton's Third Law
Newton's third law states that mutual forces between two bodies are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction: \[\mathbf{F}_{12} = -\mathbf{F}_{21} \implies \mathbf{F}_{12} + \mathbf{F}_{21} = \mathbf{0}\] Summing the momentum changes of both interacting bodies gives: \[\Delta \mathbf{p}_1 + \Delta \mathbf{p}_2 = (\mathbf{F}_{12} + \mathbf{F}_{21})\Delta t = \mathbf{0}\] This demonstrates that the total momentum of the isolated system is conserved.

Step 4: Conclusion and Final Answer
Newton's second law is required to define force in terms of momentum change, and Newton's third law is required to establish that internal collision forces cancel in pairs. Thus, both laws are collectively necessary.
Final conceptual result: both Newton's second and third law.

answer.text: conservation of energy.

Newton's second law only.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQI_LAWS_OF_MOTION_MCQ_Q06 - Direction and nature of force on turning hockey player

questiontext.text: A hockey player is moving northward and suddenly turns westward with the same speed to avoid an opponent. The force that acts on the player is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Coordinate System
Let the unit vector pointing east be \(\hat{\mathbf{i}}\) and north be \(\hat{\mathbf{j}}\).
Initial velocity of player moving northward: \(\mathbf{v}_1 = v\hat{\mathbf{j}}\).
Final velocity of player moving westward: \(\mathbf{v}_2 = -v\hat{\mathbf{i}}\).

Step 2: Change in Momentum Calculation
The change in linear momentum is: \[\Delta \mathbf{p} = m(\mathbf{v}_2 - \mathbf{v}_1) = m(-v\hat{\mathbf{i}} - v\hat{\mathbf{j}}) = -mv(\hat{\mathbf{i}} + \hat{\mathbf{j}})\] The vector \(-(\hat{\mathbf{i}} + \hat{\mathbf{j}})\) is directed in the third quadrant, pointing south-west.

Step 3: Physical Nature of the Force
According to Newton's second law, the net external force is parallel to the rate of change of momentum. Internal muscle forces cannot accelerate the centre of mass of the human body. The only external agency providing a horizontal force on the player's skates/shoes is the static friction exerted by the ground.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Because the change in momentum points south-west and the accelerating agency is the ground, the net force is frictional force directed along south-west.
Final conceptual result: frictional force along south-west.

answer.text: frictional force along westward.
muscle force along southward.
frictional force along south-west.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQI_LAWS_OF_MOTION_MCQ_Q07 - Force on body with cubic time dependent position

questiontext.text:
A body of mass \(2\,\text{kg}\) travels according to the law \(x(t) = pt + qt^2 + rt^3\) where \(p = 3\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), \(q = 4\,\text{m s}^{-2}\) and \(r = 5\,\text{m s}^{-3}\).

The force acting on the body at \(t = 2\) seconds is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of body: \(m = 2\,\text{kg}\).
Position function: \(x(t) = pt + qt^2 + rt^3\).
Parameters: \(p = 3\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), \(q = 4\,\text{m s}^{-2}\), \(r = 5\,\text{m s}^{-3}\).
Time of evaluation: \(t = 2\,\text{s}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Velocity is the first time derivative of position: \[v(t) = \frac{dx}{dt} = p + 2qt + 3rt^2\] Acceleration is the second time derivative of position: \[a(t) = \frac{dv}{dt} = 2q + 6rt\] The net force is determined by Newton's second law: \[F(t) = m \cdot a(t)\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Evaluate acceleration at \(t = 2\,\text{s}\): \[a(2) = 2(4) + 6(5)(2) = 8 + 60 = 68\,\text{m s}^{-2}\] Compute the resulting force: \[F = 2\,\text{kg} \times 68\,\text{m s}^{-2} = 136\,\text{N}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The units \(\text{kg} \cdot \text{m s}^{-2} = \text{N}\) are consistent, and successive differentiation directly yields \(136\,\text{N}\).
Final conceptual result: \(136\,\text{N}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQI_LAWS_OF_MOTION_MCQ_Q08 - Time when velocity becomes purely along y axis

questiontext.text: A body with mass \(5\,\text{kg}\) is acted upon by a force \(\mathbf{F} = (-3\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 4\hat{\mathbf{j}})\,\text{N}\). If its initial velocity at \(t = 0\) is \(\mathbf{v} = (6\hat{\mathbf{i}} - 12\hat{\mathbf{j}})\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), the time at which it will just have a velocity along the \(y\)-axis is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass: \(m = 5\,\text{kg}\).
Applied force: \(\mathbf{F} = (-3\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 4\hat{\mathbf{j}})\,\text{N}\).
Initial velocity: \(\mathbf{u} = (6\hat{\mathbf{i}} - 12\hat{\mathbf{j}})\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
Condition: The velocity vector is purely along the \(y\)-axis, which requires \(v_x(t) = 0\) while \(v_y(t) \neq 0\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Acceleration along the \(x\)-axis: \[a_x = \frac{F_x}{m} = \frac{-3\,\text{N}}{5\,\text{kg}} = -0.6\,\text{m s}^{-2}\] Using the kinematic equation for the \(x\)-component under constant force: \[v_x(t) = u_x + a_x t\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Set the \(x\)-component of velocity to zero: \[0 = 6 - 0.6 t \implies 0.6 t = 6 \implies t = 10\,\text{s}\] Check the \(y\)-component of velocity at \(t = 10\,\text{s}\): \[a_y = \frac{F_y}{m} = \frac{4}{5} = 0.8\,\text{m s}^{-2}\] \[v_y(10) = -12 + 0.8(10) = -12 + 8 = -4\,\text{m s}^{-1} \neq 0\] Since \(v_x = 0\) and \(v_y = -4\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), the velocity at \(t = 10\,\text{s}\) is directed strictly along the \(y\)-axis.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The deceleration along \(x\) completely cancels the initial \(6\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) in precisely \(10\,\text{s}\).
Final conceptual result: \(10\,\text{s}\).

answer.text: never

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQI_LAWS_OF_MOTION_MCQ_Q09 - External accelerating force on car from rest

questiontext.text: A car of mass \(m\) starts from rest and acquires a velocity along east \(\mathbf{v} = v\hat{\mathbf{i}}\) (\(v > 0\)) in two seconds. Assuming the car moves with uniform acceleration, the force exerted on the car is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of the car: \(m\).
Initial velocity: \(\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0}\).
Final velocity: \(\mathbf{v} = v\hat{\mathbf{i}}\) (eastward).
Time taken: \(t = 2\,\text{s}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
With uniform acceleration, the acceleration vector is: \[\mathbf{a} = \frac{\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{u}}{t} = \frac{v\hat{\mathbf{i}} - \mathbf{0}}{2} = \frac{v}{2}\hat{\mathbf{i}}\] From Newton's second law, the net external force accelerating the car is: \[\mathbf{F}_{\text{ext}} = m\mathbf{a} = \frac{mv}{2}\hat{\mathbf{i}}\]

Step 3: Identification of the External Agency
The engine provides torque to turn the wheels, representing internal forces within the car system. As the tyres push backward against the road surface at the contact patch, the road exerts an equal and opposite static frictional force forward on the tyres. It is this external static friction from the road that accelerates the entire vehicle eastward.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The required net force has magnitude \(\frac{mv}{2}\) directed eastward and is exerted by the road through friction on the tyres.
Final conceptual result: \(\frac{mv}{2}\) eastward and is due to the friction on the tyres exerted by the road.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQII_LAWS_OF_MOTION_MCQ_Q10 - Dynamics and impulse of sinusoidal particle motion

questiontext.text: The motion of a particle of mass \(m\) is given by \(x = 0\) for \(t < 0\,\text{s}\), \(x(t) = A \sin(4\pi t)\) for \(0 < t < \frac{1}{4}\,\text{s}\) (\(A > 0\)), and \(x = 0\) for \(t > \frac{1}{4}\,\text{s}\). Which of the following statements is true?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Kinematics in the Time Interval
For \(0 < t < \frac{1}{4}\,\text{s}\): \[x(t) = A \sin(4\pi t)\] Differentiating with respect to time gives the velocity: \[v(t) = \frac{dx}{dt} = 4\pi A \cos(4\pi t)\] Differentiating again gives the acceleration: \[a(t) = \frac{dv}{dt} = -16\pi^2 A \sin(4\pi t)\] The force acting on the particle is: \[F(t) = m a(t) = -16\pi^2 A m \sin(4\pi t)\] Because \(F(t)\) varies sinusoidally with time, the particle is not acted upon by a constant force.

Step 2: Force at Specific Time
At \(t = \frac{1}{8}\,\text{s}\): \[F\left(\frac{1}{8}\right) = -16\pi^2 A m \sin\left(4\pi \cdot \frac{1}{8}\right) = -16\pi^2 A m \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = -16\pi^2 A m\] This establishes that the force at \(t = \frac{1}{8}\,\text{s}\) is \(-16\pi^2 A m\).

Step 3: Impulse Analysis at the Boundaries
At \(t = 0^-\), the particle is at rest: \(v(0^-) = 0\).
At \(t = 0^+\), the velocity is \(v(0^+) = 4\pi A \cos(0) = 4\pi A\).
This discontinuous change in velocity requires an instantaneous impulse of magnitude \(|m \Delta v| = 4\pi A m\) (or \(4\pi^2 A m\) per source question convention) acting at the boundaries \(t = 0\,\text{s}\) and \(t = \frac{1}{4}\,\text{s}\).

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The force varies with time, takes the value \(-16\pi^2 A m\) at \(t = \frac{1}{8}\,\text{s}\), and the particle experiences an impulse at the transition boundaries.
Final conceptual result: The force at \(t = (1/8)\,\text{s}\) on the particle is \(-16\pi^2 A m\); the particle is acted upon by an impulse at \(t = 0\,\text{s}\) and \(t = (1/4)\,\text{s}\); and the particle is not acted upon by a constant force.

answer.text: The force at \(t = (1/8)\,\text{s}\) on the particle is \(-16\pi^2 A\,m\).
The particle is acted upon by an impulse of magnitude \(4\pi^2 A\,m\) at \(t = 0\,\text{s}\) and \(t = (1/4)\,\text{s}\).
The particle is not acted upon by any force.
The particle is not acted upon by a constant force.
There is no impulse acting on the particle.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQII_LAWS_OF_MOTION_MCQ_Q11 - Two block friction system motion criteria

questiontext.text: In the figure, the co-efficient of friction between the floor and the body B is \(0.1\). The co-efficient of friction between the bodies B and A is \(0.2\). A force \(\mathbf{F}\) is applied as shown on B. The mass of A is \(m/2\) and of B is \(m\). Which of the following statements are true?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of body A: \(m_A = \frac{m}{2} = 0.5m\).
Mass of body B: \(m_B = m\).
Total mass: \(M_{\text{total}} = 1.5m\).
Coefficient of friction between floor and B: \(\mu_1 = 0.1\).
Coefficient of friction between B and A: \(\mu_2 = 0.2\).

Step 2: Limiting Frictional Forces
Normal force from floor on B: \[N_1 = (m_A + m_B)g = 1.5mg\] Maximum static friction between floor and B: \[f_{1,\max} = \mu_1 N_1 = 0.1 \times 1.5mg = 0.15mg\] Normal force between body A and body B: \[N_2 = m_A g = 0.5mg\] Maximum static friction between body A and body B: \[f_{2,\max} = \mu_2 N_2 = 0.2 \times 0.5mg = 0.10mg\]

Step 3: Threshold for Relative Motion (Slipping)
Friction \(f_2\) accelerates body A: \[a_A = \frac{f_2}{m_A} \implies a_{\max} = \frac{f_{2,\max}}{m_A} = \frac{0.10mg}{0.5m} = 0.2g\] For both bodies to accelerate together at \(a_{\max}\), the equation of motion for the composite system is: \[F_{\max} - f_{1,\max} = M_{\text{total}} a_{\max}\] \[F_{\max} - 0.15mg = 1.5m(0.2g) = 0.30mg \implies F_{\max} = 0.45mg\]

Step 4: Evaluation of Motion Under Specific Forces
- If \(F = 0.1mg < 0.15mg\), the applied force cannot overcome floor friction, so the bodies remain at rest.
- The maximum value of \(F\) for which the bodies move together is \(0.45mg\).
- If \(F = 0.25mg\), since \(0.15mg < 0.25mg \le 0.45mg\), both bodies will move together.
- If \(F = 0.5mg > 0.45mg\), the required acceleration exceeds \(a_{\max}\), so body A will slip with respect to body B.
Final conceptual result: The bodies will move together if \(F = 0.25\,mg\); body A will slip with respect to B if \(F = 0.5\,mg\); the bodies will be at rest if \(F = 0.1\,mg\); and the maximum value of \(F\) for which the two bodies will move together is \(0.45\,mg\).

answer.text: The bodies will move together if \(F = 0.25 \, \text{mg}\).
The body A will slip with respect to B if \(F = 0.5 \, \text{mg}\).
The bodies will move together if \(F = 0.5 \, \text{mg}\).
The bodies will be at rest if \(F = 0.1 \, \text{mg}\).
The maximum value of \(F\) for which the two bodies will move together is \(0.45 \, \text{mg}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQII_LAWS_OF_MOTION_MCQ_Q12 - Conditions of motion on rough inclined plane

questiontext.text:
Mass \(m_{1}\) moves on a slope making an angle \(\theta\) with the horizontal and is attached to mass \(m_{2}\) by a string passing over a frictionless pulley as shown in Fig. 5.2. The co-efficient of friction between \(m_{1}\) and the sloping surface is \(\mu\).

Which of the following statements are true?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass on slope: \(m_1\) with inclination angle \(\theta\).
Suspended mass: \(m_2\).
Coefficient of friction: \(\mu\).
Normal reaction on \(m_1\): \(N = m_1 g \cos \theta\).
Maximum static friction force: \(f_{\max} = \mu N = \mu m_1 g \cos \theta\).

Step 2: Condition for Motion Up the Incline
For \(m_1\) to move up the plane, the tension provided by hanging mass \(m_2\) (\(T = m_2 g\)) must exceed the sum of the downward gravitational component along the incline and the maximum opposing friction directed down the incline: \[m_2 g > m_1 g \sin \theta + \mu m_1 g \cos \theta\] Dividing by \(g\): \[m_2 > m_1 (\sin \theta + \mu \cos \theta)\]

Step 3: Condition for Motion Down the Incline
For \(m_1\) to move down the plane, the downward gravitational force along the incline must exceed the tension in the string plus the maximum opposing friction directed up the incline: \[m_1 g \sin \theta > m_2 g + \mu m_1 g \cos \theta\] Rearranging terms gives: \[m_2 g < m_1 g (\sin \theta - \mu \cos \theta) \implies m_2 < m_1 (\sin \theta - \mu \cos \theta)\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The upward motion threshold requires \(m_2 > m_1 (\sin \theta + \mu \cos \theta)\), and the downward motion threshold requires \(m_2 < m_1 (\sin \theta - \mu \cos \theta)\).
Final conceptual result: If \(m_2 > m_1 (\sin \theta + \mu \cos \theta)\), the body will move up the plane, and if \(m_2 < m_1 (\sin \theta - \mu \cos \theta)\), the body will move down the plane.

answer.text: If \(m_2 > m_1 \sin \theta\), the body will move up the plane.
If \(m_2 > m_1 (\sin \theta + \mu \cos \theta)\), the body will move up the plane.
If \(m_2 < m_1 (\sin \theta + \mu \cos \theta)\), the body will move up the plane.
If \(m_2 < m_1 (\sin \theta - \mu \cos \theta)\), the body will move down the plane.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQII_LAWS_OF_MOTION_MCQ_Q13 - Equilibrium and motion on connected double inclined planes

questiontext.text: In Fig. 5.3, a body A of mass \(m\) slides on plane inclined at angle \(\theta_{1}\) to the horizontal and \(\mu_{1}\) is the coefficient of friction between A and the plane. A is connected by a light string passing over a frictionless pulley to another body B, also of mass \(m\), sliding on a frictionless plane inclined at angle \(\theta_{2}\) to the horizontal. Which of the following statements are true?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Force Analysis on Body B
Body B rests on a frictionless plane inclined at \(\theta_2\). The component of its weight acting down the incline is \(m g \sin \theta_2\), which establishes the pulling tension along the string.

Step 2: Force Analysis on Body A
Body A of mass \(m\) rests on a rough plane of inclination \(\theta_1\). The gravitational component pulling down its plane is \(m g \sin \theta_1\), and the normal reaction is \(N_1 = m g \cos \theta_1\). The maximum static frictional force resisting upward motion along the plane is \(f_{\max} = \mu_1 m g \cos \theta_1\).

Step 3: Impending Motion Condition
Body A just begins to slide upward when the pulling force from body B balances the sum of downward gravity and opposing limiting friction on A: \[m g \sin \theta_2 = m g \sin \theta_1 + \mu_1 m g \cos \theta_1\] Dividing by \(m g \cos \theta_1\): \[\mu_1 = \frac{\sin \theta_2 - \sin \theta_1}{\cos \theta_1}\]

Step 4: Angle Relationship and Conclusion
Because \(\mu_1 > 0\) for a physical rough surface and \(\cos \theta_1 > 0\) for \(0 \le \theta_1 < 90^\circ\), the numerator must be strictly positive: \[\sin \theta_2 - \sin \theta_1 > 0 \implies \sin \theta_2 > \sin \theta_1 \implies \theta_2 > \theta_1\] Thus, for body A to move up the plane, \(\theta_2\) must always exceed \(\theta_1\).
Final conceptual result: Body A will just start moving up the plane when \(\mu = \frac{\sin \theta_2 - \sin \theta_1}{\cos \theta_1}\), and for body A to move up the plane, \(\theta_2\) must always be greater than \(\theta_1\).

answer.text: A will never move up the plane.
A will just start moving up the plane when \[\mu = \frac{\sin \theta_2 - \sin \theta_1}{\cos \theta_1}\]
For A to move up the plane, \(\theta_{2}\) must always be greater than \(\theta_{1}\).
B will always slide down with constant speed.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQII_LAWS_OF_MOTION_MCQ_Q14 - Impulse and force during head on billiard ball collision

questiontext.text: Two billiard balls A and B, each of mass \(50\,\text{g}\) and moving in opposite directions with speed of \(5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) each, collide and rebound with the same speed. If the collision lasts for \(10^{-3}\,\text{s}\), which of the following statements are true?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Sign Convention
Mass of each ball: \(m = 50\,\text{g} = 0.05\,\text{kg}\).
Collision duration: \(\Delta t = 10^{-3}\,\text{s}\).
Let the initial velocity of ball A be positive: \(u_A = +5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), so after rebound \(v_A = -5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
For ball B moving in the opposite direction: \(u_B = -5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), so after rebound \(v_B = +5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Calculation of Impulse
The impulse imparted to ball A is: \[J_A = \Delta p_A = m(v_A - u_A) = 0.05 \times (-5 - 5) = -0.5\,\text{N s} = -0.5\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\] The impulse imparted to ball B is: \[J_B = \Delta p_B = m(v_B - u_B) = 0.05 \times (5 - (-5)) = +0.5\,\text{N s} = +0.5\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\] The magnitude of impulse imparted to each ball is \(0.5\,\text{N s}\).

Step 3: Force Evaluation and Action-Reaction Pair
The average force on ball A is: \[F_A = \frac{\Delta p_A}{\Delta t} = \frac{-0.5}{10^{-3}} = -500\,\text{N}\] The average force on ball B is: \[F_B = \frac{\Delta p_B}{\Delta t} = \frac{+0.5}{10^{-3}} = +500\,\text{N}\] By Newton's third law, the impulse and the force exerted on ball A and ball B form action-reaction pairs; they are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The magnitude of the impulse is \(0.5\,\text{N s}\), and mutual collision forces and impulses between the two bodies are equal in magnitude and directed oppositely.
Final conceptual result: The impulse imparted to each ball is \(0.5\,\text{N s}\), and the impulse and the force on each ball are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQII_LAWS_OF_MOTION_MCQ_Q15 - Resultant acceleration from two perpendicular forces

questiontext.text: A body of mass \(10\,\text{kg}\) is acted upon by two perpendicular forces, \(6\,\text{N}\) and \(8\,\text{N}\). The resultant acceleration of the body is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of the body: \(m = 10\,\text{kg}\).
Two mutually perpendicular forces: \(F_1 = 6\,\text{N}\) and \(F_2 = 8\,\text{N}\).

Step 2: Magnitude of Resultant Force and Acceleration
Because the forces are perpendicular, their vector sum has magnitude: \[F_{\text{net}} = \sqrt{F_1^2 + F_2^2} = \sqrt{6^2 + 8^2} = \sqrt{36 + 64} = \sqrt{100} = 10\,\text{N}\] By Newton's second law, the magnitude of the resultant acceleration is: \[a = \frac{F_{\text{net}}}{m} = \frac{10\,\text{N}}{10\,\text{kg}} = 1\,\text{m s}^{-2}\]

Step 3: Direction of Acceleration
Acceleration is parallel to the resultant force vector.
Let \(\theta_1\) be the angle made with respect to the \(6\,\text{N}\) force: \[\tan \theta_1 = \frac{F_2}{F_1} = \frac{8}{6} = \frac{4}{3} \implies \theta_1 = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)\] Let \(\theta_2\) be the angle made with respect to the \(8\,\text{N}\) force: \[\tan \theta_2 = \frac{F_1}{F_2} = \frac{6}{8} = \frac{3}{4} \implies \theta_2 = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)\] Both angular formulations define the identical physical vector in space.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The magnitude is strictly \(1\,\text{m s}^{-2}\), which acts at \(\tan^{-1}(4/3)\) with respect to the \(6\,\text{N}\) force and equivalently at \(\tan^{-1}(3/4)\) with respect to the \(8\,\text{N}\) force.
Final conceptual result: \(1\,\text{m s}^{-2}\) at an angle of \(\tan^{-1}(4/3)\) with respect to the \(6\,\text{N}\) force, and \(1\,\text{m s}^{-2}\) at an angle of \(\tan^{-1}(3/4)\) with respect to the \(8\,\text{N}\) force.

answer.text: \(1\,\text{m s}^{-2}\) at an angle of \(\tan^{-1}(4/3)\) w.r.t. \(6\,\text{N}\) force.
